pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the spa runs in this workspace. Share it with the spa manager, the front desk and every therapist and esthetician.
: the menu with price, length, what is included, how often each was given and the revenue.
: favorite treatment, skin and allergy notes, preferred pressure, visits, no-shows and spend; members marked as such.
: each appointment with therapist, room, add-ons, price and tip.
: treatments, member charges, gift card redemptions, refunds.
: every card sold, its balance and expiry.
A treatment from booking to paid
The front desk books the treatment, room and therapist, and checks the guest card for allergies.
On arrival, set the booking to
, record the tip and any retail.
Take payment (card, gift card or member credit) and press
Every morning: Dashboard, today's rooms, allergy notes for today's guests
Every afternoon: confirm tomorrow by text
Every Monday: retail count; failed member charges
Every quarter: unused gift cards, room use, slow treatments
Change the menu, prices, rooms and add-ons to your own, and delete the sample guests once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Skin and allergy notes are confidential and must be read before every treatment. When a guest mentions a new allergy, update the card at once.
Members pay monthly for one 60 minute treatment and get 15 percent off extra treatments and retail. Their monthly treatment is booked with no price. A member who wants a break is set to
Treatments this week, payments and member health.
A spa sells calm. Guests notice a warm table, fresh linens and an unhurried welcome, and they notice a rushed room just as fast. Turnover is a routine, not a scramble.
. Facials go in the facial studio; couples go in the couples suite; massage and body treatments use the Sage and Cedar rooms.
Leave 15 minutes between treatments in the same room (20 after a body wrap, which needs a shower and a full strip).
The Dashboard shows treatments by room. A room that runs far below the others is a sign to move a therapist's day or run a weekday offer.
Strip linens into the hamper; never on the floor
Wipe the table, face cradle, bolsters, stool, door handles and bottle pumps
Fresh sheets, blanket and face cradle cover; table warmer on
Check the guest card for the next treatment: allergies, pressure, pregnancy
Swap oils or products for allergies (no almond oil for nut allergies, no seaweed for shellfish)
Hot towels and stones at temperature if the next treatment uses them
Offer water or tea, show the locker room and the relaxation lounge.
The therapist collects the guest by name, confirms the treatment, any add-ons, and the pressure they like.
Ask about anything new since their last visit: skin changes, medications, injuries, pregnancy.
Wash hot with an unscented detergent and an oil remover; dry fully; fold and store closed. Count sets at closing; each room needs three sets for every treatment booked the next morning.

A guest with a nut allergy is booked in the Cedar room at 11 after a deep tissue at 9:30. The therapist strips the room, wipes down, swaps the almond massage oil for the fragrance-free grapeseed bottle, and has the room warm and ready at 10:55.

Card number written on every gift card payment

Expiry date checked, never refused for a reason the law does not allow

In December, gift cards can be a third of sales. Pre-print cards, keep a stack of envelopes, and add each sale to the table straight away. In January and February, expect redemptions; keep weekday openings for gift card guests.
The Dashboard lists cards that are unused or part used. Every quarter, look at cards sold more than six months ago and still unused, and send the buyer a friendly reminder for their recipient.
A real estate office buys a $500 card for a client. Three weeks later the client books a facial and a scrub for $265; the desk takes it off the balance, leaving $235, and marks the card
. The client books a massage before she leaves.
Guests trust the products their therapist used on them that day. A small, well-chosen retail shelf adds real income and keeps the result going at home.
Cleanser, serum and moisturizer for each main skin type you treat
Body oil and lotion matching your signature massage scents
A fragrance-free line for sensitive guests
The therapist names one or two products used in the treatment and why, with the guest's skin notes in mind.
No pressure: a sample size is a fine first step.
Every Monday the spa manager counts the shelf and the back room.
Reorder what is below two weeks of sales; order seasonal gift sets six weeks before the holidays.
Check dates on serums and sunscreens; move short-dated items to the front or a gift set.
Products used in treatments (massage oils, masks, scrubs) are counted with retail but kept separate. Track how many treatments a jar lasts so you can price add-ons honestly.
Sold items recorded on the guest's payment

A guest with rosacea enjoys her gentle facial. The esthetician recommends the fragrance-free calming serum used during the treatment and offers a sample. The guest buys the full size at checkout and asks for the same facial next month; the desk books it before she leaves.
Most spas sell retail at about double their cost. Review prices when suppliers change theirs, and look at what sold in the last quarter before ordering more of anything slow.
New team members learn the shelf in their first week: what each product does, which skin types it suits, and which guests should avoid it.
